2ec5dbc0-a359-49aa-8def-1c82ef17b9bf.implications: For a repo/rates desk, Hunt's thesis points toward a structurally higher and more volatile long-end rate regime and widening Treasury term/risk premium as deficit and interest-expense dynamics worsen — relevant to duration positioning, collateral supply dynamics, and front-end Fed-policy expectations, though his M2/velocity framework is idiosyncratic and not the market consensus.
key_claims: Hunt: FY just ended budget deficit was 6.3% of GDP versus a ~1.5% historical average for late-cycle expansions since 1960
Hunt: October 2025 interest expense was just under 20% of total federal revenues, and could reach ~20% of the total budget within about five years
Hunt: M2 money supply has grown at a 6.5% annualized rate since December, versus his calculated non-inflationary benchmark of roughly 3-3.25%
Hunt: core PCE inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for 67-68 consecutive months, with services inflation above 4%
Hunt: a typical recession would push the deficit from 6% to over 10% of GDP, given deficits have historically widened ~4 percentage points in downturns

2ec5dbc0-a359-49aa-8def-1c82ef17b9bf.one_liner: A veteran economist argues the Fed is accelerating money growth into an already-entrenched inflation problem while the fiscal deficit becomes structurally unmanageable, implying a sustained rise in long-end yields and Treasury risk premia.
2ec5dbc0-a359-49aa-8def-1c82ef17b9bf.recap: Dr. Lacey Hunt of Hoisington Investment Management tells Julia La Roche this is the most worried he's been in his 57-year career, despite the economy being at a late-cycle boom with low unemployment and record consumer/capital spending. His central concern is the federal budget deficit, which hit 6.3% of GDP in the last fiscal year versus a historical late-expansion norm of about 1.5% — four times worse than comparable prior periods. He calculates interest expense was already near 20% of federal revenues in October and projects it could hit 20% of the total budget within roughly five years, driven by rising debt and rising rates. He argues the deficit is politically intractable (citing Nobel laureate James Buchanan's work on democracies' inability to run surpluses in good times), and that any recession would push the deficit toward 10-10.5% of GDP, overwhelming national saving. On inflation, Hunt says M2 has grown at a 6.5% annualized rate since December versus his calculated non-inflationary benchmark of roughly 3-3.25% (potential growth plus Fed's 2% target, adjusted for rising velocity). He draws parallels to the Burns-era Fed of the 1970s, arguing inflation is not mean-reverting once embedded, and that the US has had 67-68 months of above-target inflation. He attributes the end of the disinflationary era to deglobalization/reshoring reversing prior economies-of-scale benefits, and warns of gradual erosion of dollar reserve-currency status and rising Treasury risk premia as foreign central banks diversify into gold.
terms: M2 -- a broad measure of US money supply including cash, checking/savings deposits, and retail money market funds
CPI -- Consumer Price Index, a measure of inflation based on a basket of consumer goods and services
PCE -- Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge
CBO -- Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan US agency that scores federal budget and legislative costs
